  • The inserted 35S enhancers act over long distances ($>3\text{ kb}$) in an orientation-independent manner to cause transcriptional hyperactivation and ectopic overexpression of nearby endogenous genes.
  • Because overexpressing an endogenous gene typically produces a dominant gain-of-function phenotype, mutants can be identified directly in the $T_1$ generation.
  • Enhancer/gene trapping uses promoterless reporter genes (GUS/GFP) to reveal endogenous expression patterns rather than overexpressing flanking genes.

question: Which one of the following organisms is used by plant biologists to study translocation in phloem?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Aphid Stylet Technique for Phloem Translocation Studies:
  • Aphid Feeding Mechanism: Aphids (such as Aphis fabae) are phloem-feeding hemipteran insects. They insert their ultra-fine piercing mouthparts (stylets) intercellularly through plant tissues, puncturing a single sieve tube element with minimal mechanical damage or wound callose deposition.
  • Because phloem sap is under high positive turgor pressure ($10\text{--}30\text{ atm}$), pure, uncontaminated phloem sap exudes spontaneously through the severed aphid stylet (stylet exudation technique).
  • This elegant method allowed plant physiologists to directly analyze phloem sap velocity, composition (sucrose, amino acids, signaling RNAs, proteins), and osmotic gradients.

question: In a genetic transformation experiment, a researcher failed to add the antibiotic selection agent in the shoot regeneration medium for selection of transgenic plants. In the absence of any other confounding factors, which one of the following statements is expected to be correct? Ans. B Ans. C Please visit.... www.easybiologyclass.com www.easybiologyclass.com
options: The number of regenerating shoots would be reduced in this experiment as compared to those in which the antibiotic is added.
The number of regenerating shoots is comparable to results obtained in the “negative control” of the experiment.
Transgenic plants cannot be generated from the above experiment.
The regenerating shoots would consist of a mixture of transgenic and non-transgenic plants.
correct_answer: The regenerating shoots would consist of a mixture of transgenic and non-transgenic plants.
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Role of Selectable Markers in Plant Tissue Culture Regeneration:
  • In standard plant transformation protocols, explants are co-cultivated with Agrobacterium or bombarded with DNA, where only a tiny fraction ($<1\text{--}5\%$) of cells stably integrate the transgene construct.
  • Selective Antibiotic: Inclusion of a selective agent (such as kanamycin or hygromycin) in the regeneration medium kills or arrests the division of non-transformed cells, allowing only transformed cells expressing the resistance marker to form shoots.
  • Absence of Selection: If the researcher forgets to add the antibiotic selection agent, non-transformed cells (which represent the overwhelming majority of explant cells) as well as transformed cells will both proliferate and regenerate shoots. As a result, the regenerated shoots will consist of a mixture of transgenic and non-transgenic (escapes) plants.

question: Orientation of a cloned passenger gene cassette in a binary plasmid vector, containing the expression cassette of a selectable marker gene, can be checked by PCR using
options: a combination of passenger gene-specific and vector-specific primers
correct_answer: a combination of passenger gene-specific and vector-specific primers
explanation:
[CONCEPT] PCR Verification of Insert Orientation in Cloning:
  • When a passenger gene cassette is cloned into a binary vector (for example, into a single non-directional restriction site), the inserted cassette can insert in either the sense or antisense orientation relative to vector promoter/terminator elements.
  • Checking Orientation:
    • Using only passenger gene-specific primers amplifies the internal gene fragment regardless of its orientation in the vector.
    • Using only vector-specific primers amplifies the vector backbone across the multiple cloning site regardless of insert orientation.
    • By using one passenger gene-specific primer combined with one vector-specific primer, an amplicon of a specific predicted size is generated only if the insert is in the specified orientation. If the insert is in the reverse orientation, the primers face the same direction or produce an entirely different amplicon size!

question: Somatic hybrid plants with full or nearly full complement of the two parental species are called
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Classification of Somatic Hybrid Plants:
  • Somatic Hybridization (Protoplast Fusion): Fusion of isolated somatic protoplasts from two distinct plant species or cultivars to combine their nuclear and cytoplasmic genomes.
  • Symmetric Hybrids: Somatic hybrids that retain the full or nearly full chromosomal complement of both parental species (amphidiploid/allotetraploid state).
  • Asymmetric Hybrids: Hybrids generated when one parent's protoplasts are irradiated with X-rays or gamma rays prior to fusion to selectively fragment and eliminate most of its nuclear chromosomes, transferring only a few desirable donor chromosomes or genetic traits into the recipient parent.
  • Cybrids (Cytoplasmic Hybrids): Possess the complete nuclear genome of one parent and the chloroplasts/mitochondria of both or the other parent.

question: In CAGE,
options: only 5′-end information of the transcript is analysed
only 3′-end information of the transcript is analysed
both 5′-end and 3'-end information of the transcript are analysed
complete exonic sequence of the transcript is analysed.
correct_answer: only 5′-end information of the transcript is analysed
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Cap Analysis of Gene Expression (CAGE):
  • CAGE Technology: A high-throughput sequencing-based method designed specifically for genome-wide profiling of transcription start sites (TSS) and promoter activity.
  • Mechanism:
    • Full-length mRNAs are selected by trapping their $5'$-cap structure ($m^7G$ cap).
    • A restriction enzyme (such as MmeI or EcoP15I) cuts at a defined distance ($20\text{--}27\text{ bp}$) downstream of the cap, liberating short $5'$-end sequence tags ("CAGE tags").
    • These tags are sequenced and mapped to the reference genome to pinpoint exact transcription start sites at single-nucleotide resolution and quantify transcript expression levels.
  • Therefore, CAGE analyzes only the $5'$-end information of the transcript.

question: Which one of the following statements about associative nitrogen fixing bacteria is NOT true?
options: Rhodobacter and Rhodospirillum are autotrophic photosynthetic N- fixing bacteria
Clostridium, Desulfotomaculum and Desulfovibrio are heterotrophic anaerobic N-fixing bacteria
Azospirillum is an associative autotrophic microaerophilic nitrogen fixing bacteria
Beijerinckia is an heterotrophic aerobic associative nitrogen fixing bacteria
correct_answer: Azospirillum is an associative autotrophic microaerophilic nitrogen fixing bacteria
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Physiology of Nitrogen-Fixing Bacteria:
  • Azospirillum: A well-known associative diazotroph that colonizes the rhizosphere and root interior (endosphere) of grasses, maize, rice, and wheat. It is a heterotrophic, microaerophilic bacterium that utilizes organic acids (malate, succinate, lactate) as carbon and energy sources—it is NOT autotrophic!
  • Rhodobacter and Rhodospirillum are purple non-sulfur anoxygenic photosynthetic bacteria capable of autotrophic/photoheterotrophic growth and $N_2$ fixation.
  • Clostridium and Desulfovibrio are free-living obligate anaerobic heterotrophic nitrogen fixers.
  • Beijerinckia is an aerobic heterotrophic free-living/associative nitrogen fixer common in acidic tropical soils.

question: According to the Seeds Act of 1966, which one of the following functions is NOT applicable to a Seed Certification Agency?
options: It should be an autonomous body.
It should involve itself in the production and marketing of seeds.
It should have close linkages with technical and other related institutions.
Its long-term objective should be to operate on no-profit no-loss basis.
correct_answer: It should involve itself in the production and marketing of seeds.
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Provisions of the Seeds Act, 1966 and Seed Certification Agencies:
  • Role of Seed Certification Agency: Under Section 8 of the Indian Seeds Act, 1966, a Seed Certification Agency is established to certify that agricultural seeds meet specified standards of genetic purity, physical purity, and germination capacity.
  • Integrity & Conflict of Interest: To maintain complete impartiality, objectivity, and credibility, a certification agency must be an independent, autonomous statutory body operating on a no-profit, no-loss basis. It must NOT involve itself in the commercial production or marketing of seeds.
  • Engaging in seed sales would create an immediate conflict of interest between regulatory enforcement and commercial profits.

question: Which one of the combinations given below represents populations with a similar genetic composition?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Genetic Architecture of Mapping Populations:
  • Recombinant Inbred Lines (RILs): Developed by repeated self-fertilization (single-seed descent) of $F_2$ progeny for 6 to 8 generations ($F_6\text{--}F_8$). With each generation, heterozygosity halves: $$\text{Heterozygosity in } F_n = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{n-1}$$ By $F_7\text{--}F_8$, RILs are virtually $100\%$ homozygous true-breeding lines containing recombined segments of parental chromosomes.
  • Doubled Haploids (DH): Generated by microspore/anther culture to produce haploid plantlets followed by chromosome doubling with colchicine. This achieves $100\%$ complete homozygosity in a single generation!
  • Because both RILs and DH populations consist entirely of immortal, true-breeding homozygous genotypes without segregation upon selfing, they share a very similar genetic composition.

question: Which one of the following statements represents a correct definition of Gene Pyramiding?
options: Introducing different genes for resistance to a specific pest in a single genotype
Introducing different genes for resistance to a specific pest in different genotypes
Introducing a single gene for resistance to multiple pests in a single genotype
Introducing multiple genes conferring resistance to multiple pests in different genotypes.
correct_answer: Introducing different genes for resistance to a specific pest in a single genotype
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Concept of Gene Pyramiding:
  • Definition: Gene pyramiding is the strategy of introgressing multiple distinct resistance genes (or QTLs) conferring resistance against the same specific pest or pathogen into a single plant cultivar/genotype.
  • Example: Pyramiding bacterial blight resistance genes in rice: combining xa5, xa13, and Xa21 into elite mega-varieties (such as Improved Pusa Basmati 1) to provide broad-spectrum, durable resistance that cannot be overcome by a single race of Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae.

question: A marker closely linked to the gene of interest for an agronomic trait will be used for
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Foreground vs. Background Selection in Marker-Assisted Backcrossing (MABC):
  • Foreground Selection: Uses molecular markers closely linked to (or located within) the target gene of interest to confirm the presence of the desired donor allele during backcross generations.
  • Background Selection: Uses markers distributed across the non-target chromosomes to select progeny that have the highest proportion of the recurrent parent genome (minimizing linkage drag).
  • Therefore, a marker closely linked to the gene of interest for an agronomic trait is used strictly for foreground selection.

question: The vitrification of cultured explants is generally caused by
options: low light irradiance, high temperature and intensive sterilization
high auxin, low temperature and high light irradiance
high agar, high nutrients and high pH
low pH, low temperature and low micronutrient concentration
correct_answer: low light irradiance, high temperature and intensive sterilization
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Vitrification (Hyperhydricity) in Plant Tissue Culture:
  • Vitrification (Hyperhydricity): A physiological malformation in in vitro cultured shoots characterized by translucent, water-soaked, thick, brittle, and glassy leaves with impaired stomatal functioning and reduced chlorophyll content.
  • Causative Factors: Triggered by physical and chemical stresses in culture vessels, notably:
    • High relative humidity and poor gas exchange inside vessels.
    • Sub-optimal environmental conditions: low light irradiance and high temperatures.
    • Chemical stress: severe hypochlorite/sterilant exposure (intensive sterilization), high cytokinin-to-auxin ratio, and low agar concentration (high water availability).

question: The Rht mutations in wheat that were pivotal for 'Green Revolution' reduce plant height due to impairment in
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Molecular Mechanism of Green Revolution Wheat Dwarfism (Rht Genes):
  • Rht Mutations: The semi-dwarf wheat varieties developed by Norman Borlaug that sparked the Green Revolution carry the mutant alleles Rht-B1b (formerly Rht1) or Rht-D1b (formerly Rht2).
  • DELLA Protein Function: The Rht genes encode DELLA domain transcriptional repressors that inhibit stem elongation. In wild-type wheat, binding of active gibberellin (GA) to its GID1 receptor targets DELLA proteins for ubiquitination and degradation by the 26S proteasome, permitting stem growth.
  • The Rht mutations introduce premature stop codons in the DELLA regulatory domain, producing truncated repressor proteins that cannot be degraded by GA signaling (GA-insensitive dwarfism). Thus, height reduction is caused by impairment in the gibberellic acid signaling pathway.

question: Steady state for a closed system implies
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Thermodynamic Definition of Steady State in a Closed System:
  • Closed System: A thermodynamic system that can exchange energy (heat, work) with its surroundings but cannot exchange matter (mass).
  • Steady State: A condition where all state variables (temperature, pressure, composition, density) at every point in the system remain invariant with time: $$\frac{dM}{dt} = 0, \quad \frac{dE}{dt} = 0, \quad \frac{dS_{\text{system}}}{dt} = 0$$
  • For an open system with mass flows, steady state means $\text{Input} = \text{Output}$. However, for a closed system (where mass input and output are identically zero), steady state means no net fluxes or driving forces exist within the system, meaning the system is in thermodynamic equilibrium.

question: In a lab scale reactor, the size of the air bubbles in the reactor is primarily determined by
options: size of the holes in the sparger
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Determinants of Bubble Size in Bioreactors:
  • In sparged stirred-tank bioreactors, air is introduced through a sparger at the bottom, creating primary bubbles.
  • Impeller Shear and Breakup: As these primary bubbles rise into the impeller swept zone, high hydrodynamic shear forces and turbulent kinetic energy created by the rotating impeller tear the bubbles apart into much smaller secondary micro-bubbles.
  • The maximum stable bubble diameter ($d_{\max}$) in turbulent flow is governed by the equilibrium between surface tension forces and turbulent inertial stress (Hinze criteria): $$d_{\max} \propto \left(\frac{\sigma}{\rho}\right)^{3/5} \varepsilon^{-2/5}$$ where energy dissipation rate $\varepsilon \propto N^3 D^2$.
  • Thus, agitator speed ($N$) is the primary operating variable that dictates bubble size and gas-liquid interfacial area ($a$).

question: Generally fungal fermentations are pseudoplastic. Hence in large reactors the cells
options: are better aerated near walls of the reactor
are better aerated in the centre of the reactor
get better aerated at the top rather than bottom
correct_answer: are better aerated in the centre of the reactor
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Rheology of Fungal Fermentations and Reactor Aeration:
  • Pseudoplastic (Shear-Thinning) Broths: Fungal and actinomycete fermentations (e.g., Aspergillus, Penicillium) develop dense, entangled mycelial networks that exhibit pseudoplastic, shear-thinning non-Newtonian flow behavior.
  • Spatial Viscosity Variations:
    • Near the impeller in the center of the reactor, shear rates ($\dot{\gamma}$) are very high, causing apparent viscosity to drop precipitously (thinning effect). Fluid turbulence and gas dispersion are maximal here, promoting fine bubble breakup and high oxygen transfer rates ($K_L a$).
    • Near the walls and baffles, shear rates are low, leading to extremely high apparent broth viscosity and formation of stagnant "dead zones" with poor gas hold-up and oxygen starvation.
  • Consequently, fungal cells are significantly better aerated in the centre of the reactor.

question: Mixing time increases with the volume of the reactor because of increase in the
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Scale-Up and Mixing Time in Bioreactors:
  • Mixing Time ($t_m$): The time required to achieve a specified degree of homogeneity (typically $95\%$) after adding a pulse of tracer/nutrient to the vessel.
  • Circulation Time ($t_c$): The average time required for a fluid packet to complete a closed circulation loop through the impeller zone and back: $$t_c = \frac{V}{Q} = \frac{V}{N_q N D^3}$$
  • Upon geometric scale-up at constant power per unit volume ($P/V$), the circulation path length increases with vessel diameter ($D$), causing circulation time ($t_c$) to increase dramatically. Because mixing time is directly proportional to circulation time ($t_m \approx 4\text{--}5 \times t_c$), mixing time increases with reactor volume because of the increase in circulation time.

question: The Reynolds number is a ratio of
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Physical Significance of the Reynolds Number ($Re$):
  • The Reynolds number ($Re$) is the most fundamental dimensionless group in fluid mechanics, defined as: $$Re = \frac{\rho v L}{\mu} = \frac{\text{Inertial Forces}}{\text{Viscous Forces}}$$
  • Physical Meaning:
    • Inertial forces: Represent fluid momentum and kinetic energy ($F_i \sim \rho v^2 L^2$) that promote instability, mixing, and turbulence.
    • Viscous forces: Represent internal fluid friction and shear stress ($F_v \sim \mu v L$) that dampen disturbances and maintain smooth laminar streamlines.
  • When $Re$ is large, inertial forces dominate, resulting in turbulent flow. When $Re$ is small, viscous forces dominate, resulting in laminar flow.

question: The equation τ = μ du/dy is also termed as
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Newton's Law of Viscosity and Momentum Flux:
  • Newton's law of viscosity in one-dimensional flow is given by: $$\tau_{yx} = -\mu \frac{du_x}{dy} \quad \text{or} \quad \tau = \mu \frac{du}{dy}$$
  • Physical Interpretation:
    • $\tau$ is the shear stress (force per unit area, $\text{N/m}^2$).
    • By definition, force equals the time rate of change of momentum ($\text{N} = \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}/\text{s}^2 = (\text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s})/\text{s}$).
    • Therefore, force per unit area has the units of $\frac{\text{momentum}}{\text{time} \cdot \text{area}}$, which represents the flux of momentum (rate of $x$-directed momentum transferred per unit area in the $y$-direction perpendicular to flow).
  • Hence, the equation is fundamentally known as the momentum flux equation.

question: Match the Transport process with appropriate time constants given below. Transport process Time constants 1. Oxygen transfer p. V/Q 2. Heat transfer q. 4V/(1.5ND3) 3. Flow r. VρCp/UA 4. Mixing s. 1/KLa Where V is volume; Q is pumping rate; N is agitation rate; D is diameter of the impeller; A is area and ρ is the density of the liquid
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Characteristic Time Constants of Bioreactor Transport Processes:
  • 1. Oxygen Transfer: The rate of volumetric gas-liquid oxygen mass transfer is governed by $K_L a$. The characteristic time constant is the reciprocal of the volumetric mass transfer coefficient: $$\tau_{\text{OT}} = \frac{1}{K_L a} \quad \implies \mathbf{1\text{-}s}$$
  • 2. Heat Transfer: Ratio of total thermal heat capacity of the liquid broth to the heat transfer rate through heat exchanger walls: $$\tau_{\text{HT}} = \frac{V \rho C_p}{U A} \quad \implies \mathbf{2\text{-}r}$$
  • 3. Flow / Residence Time: Ratio of fluid volume to volumetric pumping/feed flow rate: $$\tau_{\text{Flow}} = \frac{V}{Q} \quad \implies \mathbf{3\text{-}p}$$
  • 4. Mixing Time: For a stirred vessel, mixing time is proportional to circulation time: $$\tau_{\text{Mixing}} = \frac{4V}{1.5 N D^3} \quad \implies \mathbf{4\text{-}q}$$
  • Matching: 1-s, 2-r, 3-p, 4-q.

question: When a liquid of density 1200 kg/m3 and viscosity 0.01 kg m-1s-1 flows through a 1 cm ID pipe at 0.2 m/s, the flow is referred as a
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Calculation of Reynolds Number for Pipe Flow:
  • Given Parameters:
    • Liquid density ($\rho$) = $1200\text{ kg/m}^3$
    • Viscosity ($\mu$) = $0.01\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^{-1}\cdot\text{s}^{-1} = 0.01\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s}$
    • Pipe internal diameter ($D$) = $1\text{ cm} = 0.01\text{ m}$
    • Average flow velocity ($v$) = $0.2\text{ m/s}$
  • Reynolds Number Formula: $$Re = \frac{\rho v D}{\mu} = \frac{1200 \times 0.2 \times 0.01}{0.01} = 1200 \times 0.2 = 240$$
  • Flow Regime Criteria in Pipes:
    • $Re < 2100 \implies$ Laminar flow
    • $2100 \le Re \le 4000 \implies$ Transition flow
    • $Re > 4000 \implies$ Turbulent flow
  • Since $Re = 240 \ll 2100$, the flow is strictly Laminar flow.

question: In a dynamic gassing out technique for determination of KLa in a bioreactor, upon restart of the aeration the increase in DO slows down with time because
options: the cultures specific OUR declines to reach a steady state
KLa changes when the cells get sufficient oxygen supply
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Dynamic Gassing-Out Technique for $K_L a$ Measurement:
  • In the dynamic gassing-out method, aeration is temporarily stopped, causing the dissolved oxygen concentration ($C_L$) to drop due to cellular oxygen uptake rate ($OUR$): $$\frac{dC_L}{dt} = -OUR$$
  • When aeration is restarted, DO re-accumulates according to: $$\frac{dC_L}{dt} = K_L a (C^* - C_L) - OUR$$
  • As time progresses, $C_L$ rises and gets progressively closer to the saturation concentration ($C^*$). Consequently, the concentration driving force $(C^* - C_L)$ decreases, which inherently slows down the rate of DO increase with time until a steady plateau is reached.

question: Under unaerated conditions in a fermenter, the power consumed by a single impeller is 10 KW and upon changing the agitation rate from 200 to 600 rpm, the new power consumption (KW) would be -----. (Assuming that the power number remains constant)
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Power Consumption in Stirred Tanks and Agitation Speed:
  • In bioreactor design, impeller power consumption ($P$) in the turbulent regime is governed by the Power Number ($N_p$): $$P = N_p \cdot \rho \cdot N^3 \cdot D^5$$
  • If the fluid density ($\rho$), impeller diameter ($D$), and power number ($N_p$) remain constant: $$\frac{P_2}{P_1} = \left(\frac{N_2}{N_1}\right)^3$$
  • Calculation:
    • Initial speed $N_1 = 200\text{ rpm}$, initial power $P_1 = 10\text{ kW}$
    • Final speed $N_2 = 600\text{ rpm}$
    • Speed ratio: $\frac{N_2}{N_1} = \frac{600}{200} = 3$
    • $$P_2 = P_1 \times (3)^3 = 10\text{ kW} \times 27 = \mathbf{270\text{ kW}}$$

question: Fill in the blanks with appropriate option: Vinegar is a liquid consisting of acetic acid produced by the fermentation of _______________ by _____________________.
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Biochemistry of Vinegar Production:
  • Vinegar is a dilute aqueous solution consisting primarily of $4\text{--}8\%$ acetic acid by volume.
  • Two-Stage Fermentation Process:
    • Stage 1 (Anaerobic): Yeasts (such as Saccharomyces cerevisiae) ferment sugars (from grapes, apples, or malt) anaerobically into ethanol.
    • Stage 2 (Aerobic): Acetic acid bacteria (principally Acetobacter aceti or Gluconacetobacter species) perform the obligate aerobic oxidation of ethanol into acetic acid: $$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + \text{O}_2 \xrightarrow{A.\text{ aceti}} \text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
  • Therefore, vinegar consists of acetic acid produced by the fermentation of ethanol by A. aceti.

question: A food stored in a refrigerator has caused an outbreak of food borne illness. Which one of the following is most likely to be the pathogen responsible for this?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Psychrotrophic Pathogens and Foodborne Illness:
  • Psychrotrophic Bacteria: Microorganisms capable of surviving, metabolizing, and multiplying at cold refrigeration temperatures ($0\text{--}4^\circ\text{C}$).
  • Listeria monocytogenes: A Gram-positive, non-spore-forming, facultatively anaerobic rod that is the premier psychrotrophic foodborne pathogen. It can proliferate to dangerous levels in refrigerated ready-to-eat deli meats, unpasteurized soft cheeses, and packaged salads.
  • Ingestion can cause severe listeriosis, leading to septicemia, meningitis, and spontaneous abortions in pregnant women.
  • Salmonella, E. coli, and B. cereus are mesophiles whose growth is effectively inhibited at standard refrigeration temperatures.

question: To reduce the tartness in wine due to malic acid, a secondary fermentation is carried out using
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Malolactic Fermentation in Winemaking:
  • Malic Acid Tartness: Grapes grown in cool climates contain high concentrations of L-malic acid (a harsh dicarboxylic acid), making wine taste excessively sour and astringent.
  • Secondary Fermentation: Winemakers inoculate the wine with selected lactic acid bacteria, predominantly Oenococcus oeni (formerly Leuconostoc oenos), to carry out malolactic fermentation (MLF): $$\text{L-Malic Acid } (\text{dicarboxylic}) \xrightarrow{\text{Malolactic enzyme}} \text{L-Lactic Acid } (\text{monocarboxylic}) + \text{CO}_2$$
  • Because a dicarboxylic acid is converted into a milder monocarboxylic acid, the wine's total titratable acidity decreases, pH increases by $0.1\text{--}0.3$ units, and buttery aromatic notes (diacetyl) are produced, imparting a smooth, round mouthfeel.

question: Which one of the following statements is INCORRECT with respect to food rheology?
options: Ketchup is an example of shear thinning, pseudoplastic liquid
Molten chocolate is a perfect Newtonian fluid
correct_answer: Molten chocolate is a perfect Newtonian fluid
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Rheological Behavior of Food Materials:
  • Food Rheology Classifications:
    • Yoghurt: Exhibits thixotropy (time-dependent shear-thinning; its viscosity decreases over time under constant shear and recovers upon resting). (Correct)
    • Ketchup: A classic pseudoplastic (shear-thinning) liquid exhibiting a yield stress; shaking the bottle reduces its viscosity so it pours freely. (Correct)
    • Wheat Dough: Exhibits both viscous fluid and elastic solid properties due to the hydrated glutenin-gliadin protein network, making it classic viscoelastic. (Correct)
    • Molten Chocolate: Molten chocolate contains cocoa particles and sugar crystals dispersed in a continuous cocoa butter fat phase. It behaves as a non-Newtonian fluid exhibiting a yield stress followed by shear-thinning behavior (accurately described by the Casson fluid model). It is NOT a Newtonian fluid!

question: Which one of the following enzyme(s) would result in high glucose yield from starch hydrolysis?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Enzymatic Hydrolysis of Starch to High D-Glucose Yield:
  • Starch consists of amylose (linear $\alpha\text{-}1,4$ glucan) and amylopectin (branched glucan with $\alpha\text{-}1,4$ linear chains and $\alpha\text{-}1,6$ branch linkages every $24\text{--}30$ residues).
  • Synergistic Enzyme Combination:
    • $\alpha$-Amylase: An endo-hydrolase that randomly cleaves internal $\alpha\text{-}1,4$ linkages in gelatinized starch, rapidly reducing viscosity and producing linear and branched dextrins/maltose (liquefaction).
    • Amyloglucosidase (Glucoamylase): An exo-hydrolase that attacks the non-reducing ends of dextrins, sequentially releasing free D-glucose units. Uniquely, amyloglucosidase hydrolyzes both $\alpha\text{-}1,4$ linkages and the stubborn $\alpha\text{-}1,6$ branch points!
  • Together, $\alpha$-amylase and amyloglucosidase convert starch almost quantitatively into pure D-glucose ($>96\%\text{ yield}$).

question: The major metabolite formed and the succession of microorganisms responsible for Sauerkraut fermentation are
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Microbial Succession in Sauerkraut Fermentation:
  • Sauerkraut is produced by the spontaneous, solid-state lactic acid fermentation of shredded salted cabbage ($2\text{--}2.5\%\text{ NaCl}$).
  • Microbial Succession:
    1. Coliforms / Aerobic Epiphytes: Initially, salt draws water and nutrients from cabbage; residual oxygen is rapidly depleted by coliform bacteria and yeasts.
    2. Leuconostoc mesenteroides: A heterofermentative lactic acid bacterium that initiates the primary fermentation, rapidly lowering pH by producing lactic acid, acetic acid, ethanol, and $\text{CO}_2$ (which establishes anaerobiosis).
    3. Lactobacillus plantarum & Lactobacillus brevis: Acid-tolerant homofermentative and heterofermentative lactobacilli complete the fermentation, driving the final pH down to $\sim 3.5\text{--}3.8$ with high yields of lactic acid.
  • Therefore, the major metabolite formed is lactic acid, and the microbial succession is Coliform $\to$ Leuconostoc $\to$ Lactobacilli.

question: Omega 3 fats are good for health and play an important role in prevention of heart disease. If you have to formulate a food product rich in omega 3 fats which one of the following options would you choose?
options: rice bran oil because it contains C 18:2 ∆9c, 12c
flax seed oil because it contains C 18:3 ∆9c, 12c, 15c
olive oil because it contains C 18:1 ∆9c
black- currant seed oil because it contains C 18:3 ∆ 6c, 9c, 12c
correct_answer: flax seed oil because it contains C 18:3 ∆9c, 12c, 15c
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Structure and Sources of Omega-3 Fatty Acids:
  • Omega-3 ($\omega\text{-}3$) Fatty Acids: Polyunsaturated fatty acids whose first double bond is situated at the third carbon atom from the methyl (omega, $\omega$) end of the hydrocarbon chain.
  • Flaxseed Oil (Linseed Oil): The richest plant-based dietary source of $\alpha$-linolenic acid (ALA): $$\text{ALA: } C18:3\,\Delta^{9c, 12c, 15c}$$ Calculating the omega position from the carboxyl end ($C=1$): $$\text{Total carbons} - \text{Position of last double bond} = 18 - 15 = \mathbf{3 \implies \omega\text{-}3}$$
  • Rice bran oil contains linoleic acid ($C18:2\,\Delta^{9c, 12c}$, which is an $\omega\text{-}6$ fatty acid: $18 - 12 = 6$).
  • Olive oil contains oleic acid ($C18:1\,\Delta^{9c}$, an $\omega\text{-}9$ monounsaturated fatty acid: $18 - 9 = 9$).

question: For a well-established enzyme assay method where the reaction kinetics should remain zero order, what percentage of substrate is converted to product during the incubation period?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Substrate Consumption in Zero-Order Enzyme Assays:
  • In quantitative clinical and biochemical enzyme assays, initial velocity ($v_0$) must be directly proportional to enzyme concentration ($[E]$). This requires true zero-order kinetics with respect to substrate ($[S] \gg K_m$, where $v \approx V_{\max} = k_{\text{cat}}[E]$).
  • If substrate is significantly depleted during the incubation period, $[S]$ drops closer to $K_m$, the reaction enters mixed/first-order kinetics, and reaction rate slows non-linearly, underestimating enzyme activity.
  • To maintain steady zero-order kinetics and linear product accumulation throughout the assay incubation, standard analytical protocols dictate that no more than $6\text{--}10\%$ of the initial substrate should be converted to product.

question: As the viscosity increases, the method used for mixing is changed in the following order
options: Paddle, Turbine, Propeller, Helical ribbon and Screw
Propeller, Turbine, Paddle, Helical ribbon and Screw
Propeller, Paddle, Turbine, Helical ribbon and Screw
Propeller, Turbine, Paddle, Screw and Helical ribbon
correct_answer: Propeller, Turbine, Paddle, Helical ribbon and Screw
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Impeller Selection Hierarchy Based on Fluid Viscosity:
  • As the viscosity of the fermentation broth increases, the flow regime transitions from turbulent to laminar, requiring impellers with larger swept diameters and lower operating speeds to avoid high power dissipation and localized stagnant zones:
    1. Propellers (Marine Propeller): High-speed, axial-flow impellers for low-viscosity fluids ($<100\text{ cP}$ or $<0.1\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s}$).
    2. Turbines (Rushton / Flat-blade turbine): High-shear, radial-flow impellers suitable for moderate viscosities ($100\text{--}10,000\text{ cP}$).
    3. Paddles: Low-to-moderate speed impellers with wide blades extending closer to the walls for medium-to-high viscosity liquids ($1,000\text{--}50,000\text{ cP}$).
    4. Helical Ribbon Impellers: Close-clearance impellers with ribbons spiraling along the wall, effective for highly viscous non-Newtonian pseudoplastic and viscoelastic fluids ($50,000\text{--}1,000,000\text{ cP}$).
    5. Screw Impellers: Central Archimedean screw impellers used for extreme viscosities, pasty masses, and heavy doughs.
  • Order: Propeller $\to$ Turbine $\to$ Paddle $\to$ Helical ribbon $\to$ Screw.

question: On scale up, the effective area available for heat transfer in a bioreactor
options: Depends on viscosity of the medium
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Scale-Up and Specific Heat Transfer Surface Area:
  • For geometrically similar stirred-tank bioreactors of diameter $D$ and liquid height $H \propto D$:
    • Bioreactor working volume scales with the cube of diameter: $V \propto D^3$.
    • Heat generation from microbial metabolism and mechanical agitation scales proportionally with volume: $Q_{\text{gen}} \propto V \propto D^3$.
    • The available surface area of the reactor wall/jacket scales only with the square of diameter: $A \propto D^2$.
  • Therefore, the effective heat transfer area per unit volume ($A/V$) is: $$\frac{A}{V} \propto \frac{D^2}{D^3} = \frac{1}{D}$$
  • As the reactor scale increases (larger $D$), the ratio of available heat transfer area to volume decreases. This makes metabolic heat removal one of the most critical limiting bottlenecks in industrial bioreactor scale-up.

question: A fermenter produces 100 kg lysine per day. If the volumetric productivity is 0.8 gl-1h-1, what is the volume of the fermenter in liter?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Bioreactor Volume Calculation from Volumetric Productivity:
  • Given:
    • Target daily production = $100\text{ kg lysine/day} = 100,000\text{ g/day}$
    • Volumetric productivity ($Q_P$) = $0.8\text{ g}\cdot\text{L}^{-1}\cdot\text{h}^{-1}$
    • Operating hours per day = $24\text{ h/day}$
  • Step 1: Calculate daily productivity per liter of working volume: $$Q_{P(\text{daily})} = 0.8\text{ g}\cdot\text{L}^{-1}\cdot\text{h}^{-1} \times 24\text{ h/day} = 19.2\text{ g}\cdot\text{L}^{-1}\cdot\text{day}^{-1}$$
  • Step 2: Calculate required bioreactor volume ($V$): $$V = \frac{\text{Total daily production}}{Q_{P(\text{daily})}} = \frac{100,000\text{ g/day}}{19.2\text{ g/L/day}} \approx 5208.3\text{ L}$$
  • Rounding to the closest standard reactor size gives 5200 L.

question: Chemostat cultivation is carried out at steady state with a dilution rate of 0.1 h-1 . Given μm = 1.1 h-1and Ks=0.1 g/L. What will be steady state substrate concentration?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Steady-State Substrate Concentration in a Chemostat:
  • In an ideal chemostat at steady state, the specific growth rate $\mu$ is set and locked by the dilution rate $D$: $$\mu = D = 0.1\text{ h}^{-1}$$
  • According to the Monod growth kinetics equation: $$\mu = \frac{\mu_m S}{K_s + S}$$
  • Derivation: $$0.1 = \frac{1.1 S}{0.1 + S}$$ $$0.1(0.1 + S) = 1.1 S$$ $$0.01 + 0.1 S = 1.1 S$$ $$1.0 S = 0.01 \implies S = 0.01\text{ g/L}$$
  • Note on Examination Keys: Exact kinetic solving yields $0.01\text{ g/L}$ (Option A). The official key published Option B ($0.1\text{ g/L}$), often due to approximated calculation ignoring $S$ in the denominator ($D \approx \mu_m S / K_s$). Both the rigorous mathematical solution ($0.01\text{ g/L}$) and official key (Option B) are noted.

question: For degradation of crude oil in ocean by microorganisms, the two limiting nutrients are
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Limiting Nutrients in Marine Hydrocarbon Bioremediation:
  • Following crude oil spills in marine environments, indigenous hydrocarbon-degrading bacteria (such as Alcanivorax borkumensis) have access to an enormous abundance of reduced organic carbon and energy.
  • However, open ocean seawater contains extremely low concentrations of bioavailable nitrogen and phosphorus. The natural stoichiometric carbon-to-nitrogen-to-phosphorus ratio required for microbial biomass synthesis is approximately $C : N : P \approx 100 : 10 : 1$.
  • The massive influx of petroleum carbon creates an acute nutrient imbalance, where nitrates (or ammonia) and phosphates become the strictly rate-limiting nutrients. Supplementation with oleophilic or slow-release N and P fertilizers dramatically accelerates oil bioremediation.

question: The first circumpolar expedition in the history of Marine Sciences was
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Historical Milestones in Marine Sciences:
  • The HMS Challenger Expedition (1872–1876): Led by Scottish marine biologist Sir Charles Wyville Thomson and the Royal Society, this was the first global circumpolar oceanographic expedition conceived solely for marine scientific research.
  • Covering nearly $70,000\text{ nautical miles}$, the expedition sounded the deepest point of the world's oceans (the Mariana Trench / Challenger Deep), collected temperature and water depth profiles, identified over 4,700 new marine species, and disproved the 'Azoic hypothesis' by proving abundant life exists in the abyssal depths.

question: Paralytic shellfish poisoning (PSP) is caused by the consumption of molluscan Shellfish contaminated with
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Marine Biotoxins and Shellfish Poisoning Syndromes:
  • Paralytic Shellfish Poisoning (PSP): Caused by Saxitoxins (potent voltage-gated sodium channel blockers produced by dinoflagellates like Alexandrium, Gymnodinium, and Pyrodinium). Shellfish filter-feed on these blooms and concentrate saxitoxins, causing rapid numbness, paralysis, and respiratory arrest in human consumers.
  • Other Shellfish Syndromes:
    • Brevetoxins: Cause Neurotoxic Shellfish Poisoning (NSP).
    • Domoic Acid: Causes Amnesic Shellfish Poisoning (ASP).
    • Okadaic Acid: Causes Diarrhetic Shellfish Poisoning (DSP).

question: Biofilm/capsular material produced by the soil bacteria is detected by
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Detection of Biofilm and Extracellular Capsule:
  • Congo Red Agar (CRA) Method: Developed by Freeman et al., Congo Red is a planar diazo dye widely used to detect biofilm and slime/capsular production in bacteria (such as Staphylococcus and soil bacteria).
  • Congo red binds specifically to extracellular amyloid fimbriae (curli), $\beta$-glucans, and exopolysaccharides (EPS) that constitute the structural scaffolding of bacterial biofilms.
  • Biofilm-producing, capsule-forming colonies display an intense, characteristic black, crystalline morphology on Congo red agar, whereas non-biofilm producers form smooth red colonies.

question: A compound secreted by a soil bacterium capable of reducing the surface tension at air-water interface is called as
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Bacterial Biosurfactants:
  • Biosurfactants: Amphiphilic surface-active compounds produced extracellularly or cell-bound by microorganisms (bacteria, yeasts, fungi).
  • They consist of a hydrophobic moiety (hydrocarbon chain of a fatty acid) and a hydrophilic moiety (carbohydrate, peptide, or phosphate group). Common examples include rhamnolipids (Pseudomonas) and surfactin (Bacillus subtilis).
  • Biosurfactants partition at the air-water and oil-water interfaces, dramatically reducing surface and interfacial tension (e.g., lowering water surface tension from $72\text{ mN/m}$ to $<30\text{ mN/m}$), enhancing the emulsification and bioavailability of insoluble hydrocarbons.

question: Match the organism in Group A with the appropriate habitat from Group B. Group A Group B P) Pseudomonas i) Hot springs Q) Thermus ii) Rhizosphere R) Photobacterium iii) Soil S) Thiobacillus iv) Marine Ans. C Ans. D Please visit.... www.easybiologyclass.com www.easybiologyclass.com
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Ecological Niches and Habitats of Microorganisms:
  • P) Pseudomonas $\to$ (ii) Rhizosphere: Highly versatile heterotrophs (e.g., P. putida, P. fluorescens) that aggressively colonize plant root exudate-rich rhizosphere zones.
  • Q) Thermus $\to$ (i) Hot springs: Extreme thermophiles (such as Thermus aquaticus, source of Taq DNA polymerase) that thrive in thermal hot springs at temperatures above $70^\circ\text{C}$.
  • R) Photobacterium $\to$ (iv) Marine: Marine bioluminescent bacteria (e.g., P. phosphoreum) inhabiting seawater and forming symbiotic light organs in deep-sea fishes.
  • S) Thiobacillus $\to$ (iii) Soil / Mineral Ores: Chemolithoautotrophic sulfur-oxidizing bacteria that populate soils, acid mine drainages, and mineral deposits.
  • Correct matching: P-ii, Q-i, R-iv, S-iii.

question: Match the type of Organism in Group A with appropriate phenotype/property from Group B. Group A Group B P) Pseudomoans aeruginosa i) Sulfur oxidizing organism Q) Staphylococcus aureus ii) Elemental N2 fixation R) Thiobacillus ferroxidance iii) Biofilm formation S) Bradyrhizobium iv) Quorum sensing
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Characteristics and Phenotypes of Selected Bacteria:
  • P) Pseudomonas aeruginosa $\to$ (iii) Biofilm formation: Produces abundant extracellular alginate matrix, forming thick, resilient biofilms in cystic fibrosis lungs and medical catheters.
  • Q) Staphylococcus aureus $\to$ (iv) Quorum sensing: Uses the Agr (accessory gene regulator) two-component autoinducing peptide (AIP) quorum-sensing system to coordinate exoprotein virulence factor production.
  • R) Thiobacillus ferrooxidans (Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans) $\to$ (i) Sulfur oxidizing organism: An obligate chemolithoautotroph that oxidizes elemental sulfur and ferrous iron to sulfuric acid and ferric iron.
  • S) Bradyrhizobium $\to$ (ii) Elemental $\text{N}_2$ fixation: Symbiotic nitrogen-fixing bacterium that forms root nodules on legumes (soybean) to fix atmospheric dinitrogen into ammonia.
  • Correct matching: P-iii, Q-iv, R-i, S-ii.

question: Which one of the following reactions is performed by Cytochrome-P450 to detoxify the xenobiotics?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Cytochrome P450 Detoxification of Xenobiotics:
  • Phase I Metabolism: The Cytochrome P450 (CYP450) superfamily of heme monooxygenases plays the central role in the biotransformation and detoxification of lipophilic foreign compounds (xenobiotics, drugs, environmental toxins).
  • Hydroxylation Reaction: CYP450 utilizes molecular oxygen and reducing equivalents from NADPH (via CYP450 reductase) to catalyze the insertion of one oxygen atom into an aliphatic or aromatic carbon-hydrogen bond, producing a hydroxyl group: $$\text{R-H} + \text{O}_2 + \text{NADPH} + \text{H}^+ \xrightarrow{\text{CYP450}} \text{R-OH} + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{NADP}^+$$
  • Hydroxylation creates a functional, polar handle that increases water solubility and allows subsequent Phase II conjugation (glucuronidation/sulfation) for excretion.

question: Which one of the following is NOT true regarding Zika virus?
options: It was first isolated in Uganda
It is transmitted by Anopheles mosquito
correct_answer: It is transmitted by Anopheles mosquito
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Zika Virus Transmission and Pathology:
  • Virology: Zika virus is an enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus belonging to the genus Flavivirus (family Flaviviridae). It was first isolated in 1947 from a rhesus macaque in the Zika Forest of Uganda.
  • Vector: Zika virus is transmitted primarily by the bite of infected daytime-active Aedes mosquitoes (principally Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus)—the same mosquitoes that transmit Dengue and Chikungunya. It is NOT transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes (which are vectors for malaria parasites).
  • Complications: Infection during pregnancy can cause congenital Zika syndrome, leading to severe fetal microcephaly and neurological abnormalities.

question: The vaccine currently used in India’s Pulse polio campaign is
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Vaccine Type Used in India's Pulse Polio Programme:
  • Pulse Polio Immunization: India's nationwide campaign to eradicate poliomyelitis relied on the Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV, Sabin vaccine).
  • Nature of OPV: OPV consists of live attenuated polioviruses (strains of Serotypes 1, 2, and 3) that have been attenuated by repeated serial passage in non-human cells.
  • Live attenuated OPV replicates in the intestinal mucosal epithelial cells, inducing robust local secretory IgA (sIgA) mucosal immunity in the gut as well as systemic IgG antibodies. This mucosal immunity effectively blocks wild poliovirus transmission in the population.
  • (The Salk vaccine, IPV, is an inactivated/killed vaccine administered by intramuscular injection).

question: Which one of the following enzymes helps in the survival of Helicobacter pylori in the stomach?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Role of Urease in Helicobacter pylori Gastric Survival:
  • Gastric Acid Challenge: Helicobacter pylori colonizes the human stomach, where gastric hydrochloric acid creates a brutally hostile environment (pH $1.5\text{--}2.0$).
  • Urease Buffer Cloud: H. pylori produces huge amounts of the nickel-dependent enzyme urease (constituting up to $10\text{--}15\%$ of its total bacterial protein). Urease hydrolyzes physiological urea into carbon dioxide and ammonia: $$\text{CO(NH}_2)_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{\text{Urease}} \text{CO}_2 + 2\text{NH}_3$$
  • Basic ammonia rapidly reacts with gastric acid ($NH_3 + H^+ \to NH_4^+$), neutralizing stomach acid in the bacterium's immediate periplasmic and microenvironmental perimeter, creating a neutral protective buffer cloud that allows colonization of gastric mucosa.

question: Which one of the following is INCORRECT about Streptokinase?
options: It was originally obtained from β hemolytic streptococci
It is used as a therapeutic anti-thrombogenic agent
It is used as a therapeutic fibrinolytic agent
correct_answer: It is used as a therapeutic anti-thrombogenic agent
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Pharmacology of Streptokinase:
  • Origin: Streptokinase is an extracellular non-enzymatic protein secreted by group C $\beta$-hemolytic streptococci (Streptococcus dysgalactiae).
  • Mechanism of Action: It is a potent therapeutic fibrinolytic (thrombolytic) agent. Streptokinase forms an equimolar complex with circulating plasminogen, inducing a conformational change that converts other plasminogen molecules into active plasmin, which degrades and dissolves existing fibrin blood clots (thrombi).
  • Antigenicity: Because it is a bacterial protein, it is highly antigenic/immunogenic in humans; repeated administration can trigger neutralizing antistreptococcal antibodies or anaphylaxis.
  • Incorrect Description: Streptokinase is a thrombolytic agent used to lyse pre-existing acute clots (e.g., in acute myocardial infarction). It is NOT an anti-thrombogenic agent (anti-thrombogenic agents prevent initial platelet aggregation or thrombus formation on biomedical surfaces or vessels).

question: The utility of positron emission tomography to diagnose tumors is based on
options: activation of hypoxia-inducible transcription factor HIF-1
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Principles of Positron Emission Tomography (PET) in Oncology:
  • The Warburg Effect: Cancer cells undergo metabolic reprogramming characterized by exceptionally high rates of aerobic glycolysis and dramatic upregulation of glucose transporters (GLUT1 and GLUT3) and hexokinase enzymes.
  • Radiotracer: Clinical oncology PET imaging exploits this metabolic phenotype using $^{18}\text{F}$-FDG (2-fluoro-2-deoxyglucose), a glucose analog labeled with positron-emitting Fluorine-18.
  • Metabolic Trapping: $^{18}\text{F}$-FDG is avidly transported into tumor cells by GLUT transporters and phosphorylated by hexokinase into $^{18}\text{F}$-FDG-6-phosphate. Because it lacks a $2'-$hydroxyl group, it cannot be metabolized further by phosphoglucose isomerase and cannot exit the cell, becoming "metabolically trapped" inside tumor cells, creating high-contrast PET signals.

question: Which one of the following imaging techniques is non-invasive?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Non-Invasive Diagnostic Imaging Modalities:
  • Ultrasound Imaging (Sonography): Uses high-frequency sound waves ($2\text{--}18\text{ MHz}$) transmitted into the body via an external acoustic transducer placed on the skin with coupling gel. It utilizes no ionizing radiation, radioactive tracers, or injected intravascular dyes, making it completely non-invasive and safe (even for obstetric fetal monitoring).
  • Contrast CT: Requires intravenous administration of iodinated radiocontrast media (invasive injection, risk of contrast-induced nephropathy/anaphylaxis) and exposes the patient to ionizing X-ray radiation.
  • Nuclear Imaging (Scintigraphy) & PET Imaging: Require intravenous injection of radioactive radiopharmaceuticals (e.g., $^{99m}\text{Tc}$, $^{18}\text{F}$-FDG), making them invasive procedures involving ionizing radiation.

question: Amphotericin B is clinically used against which one of the following pathogens?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Antifungal Spectrum and Mechanism of Amphotericin B:
  • Amphotericin B: A polyene macrolide antibiotic produced naturally by the soil actinomycete Streptomyces nodosus. It remains the gold-standard therapeutic agent for life-threatening systemic fungal infections.
  • Mechanism of Action: Amphotericin B selectively binds with high affinity to ergosterol, the principal sterol component in fungal plasma membranes. This creates transmembrane barrel-stave pores/channels that cause leakage of intracellular monovalent ions ($\text{K}^+, \text{Na}^+$), disrupting electrochemical gradients and precipitating rapid fungal cell lysis and death.
  • Clinical Application: Extensively used to treat invasive candidiasis (infections caused by Candida spp.), cryptococcal meningitis, systemic aspergillosis, and mucormycosis. It has no antiviral, antibacterial, or antiparasitic activity against HSV-1, M. tuberculosis, or P. vivax.

question: The therapeutic index (TI) indicates the relative margin of safety of a drug and it is deduced from the values of mean lethal dose (LD50) and median effective dose (ED50). Which of the following represents TI of a drug?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Definition and Calculation of the Therapeutic Index (TI):
  • Therapeutic Index (TI): A quantitative pharmacological measurement that reflects the relative margin of safety and selectivity of a drug.
  • Formula: In preclinical animal pharmacology, the therapeutic index is defined as the ratio of the median lethal dose to the median effective dose: $$\mathbf{TI = \frac{LD_{50}}{ED_{50}}}$$
  • Interpretation:
    • $\text{LD}_{50}$ is the dose of drug that proves lethal to $50\%$ of the tested animal population.
    • $\text{ED}_{50}$ is the dose of drug that produces the desired therapeutic effect in $50\%$ of the population.
    • A larger TI indicates a wide margin of safety (a large difference between the therapeutic dose and toxic dose, e.g., penicillin), whereas a small TI indicates a narrow margin of safety requiring close therapeutic drug monitoring (e.g., digoxin, warfarin, lithium).

question: Which one of the following is a frequently used radio-opaque dye?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Radio-Opaque Contrast Agents in Radiology:
  • Barium Sulphate ($\text{BaSO}_4$): The most widely utilized radio-opaque contrast medium for radiological examination of the human gastrointestinal (GI) tract (such as barium swallow, barium meal, and barium enema procedures).
  • Physical Basis: Barium has a high atomic number ($Z = 56$), meaning its dense electron cloud strongly attenuates and absorbs X-ray photons through the photoelectric effect, casting a brilliant white, radiopaque silhouette on radiographic film and fluoroscopic screens.
  • Safety: Unlike water-soluble barium salts (like $\text{BaCl}_2$ or $\text{Ba(NO}_3)_2$), which are highly neurotoxic and cardiotoxic because soluble $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ ions block potassium channels, barium sulphate is virtually insoluble in water and gastric acid ($K_{\text{sp}} \approx 1.1 \times 10^{-10}$), passing safely through the GI tract without systemic absorption.

question: The name of the blood vessel marked [?] in the figure below is
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Anatomy of the Human Heart and Great Vessels:
  • Pulmonary Circulation: Deoxygenated systemic venous blood enters the right atrium via the superior and inferior vena cava, flows through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, and is pumped during ventricular systole into the Pulmonary Artery (pulmonary trunk).
  • The pulmonary artery branches into left and right pulmonary arteries to transport deoxygenated blood to the lungs for alveolar gas exchange.
  • Oxygenated blood returns from the lungs to the left atrium via the four pulmonary veins.
  • In cardiac anatomical diagrams, the great vessel emerging anteriorly from the right ventricle arching toward the lungs is the pulmonary artery.

question: Which one of the following is a reason for administering general anesthesia to experimental animals?
options: It reduces the toxicity of a test drug
It provides reasonable degree of muscle relaxation
It maintains the normal level of haemoglobin
It maintains the normal body temperature
correct_answer: It provides reasonable degree of muscle relaxation
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Physiological Goals of General Anesthesia in Animals:
  • General anesthesia in experimental animal surgery is administered to achieve a reversible state of profound central nervous system depression characterized by:
    1. Unconsciousness: Loss of awareness and voluntary responses.
    2. Analgesia: Complete insensitivity to surgical pain.
    3. Muscle Relaxation: A reasonable degree of skeletal muscle relaxation, which prevents reflex twitching, spasticity, and abdominal wall tension, allowing smooth surgical access and organ manipulation.
    4. Amnesia and Areflexia: Suppression of autonomic stress reflexes.
  • Anesthesia does not reduce drug toxicity, nor does it maintain normal body temperature (in fact, general anesthetics impair thermoregulation and frequently cause hypothermia requiring heating pads).

question: During the pathogenesis of rabies, the replication of virus first starts in the
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Pathogenesis and Neurotropism of Rabies Virus:
  • Inoculation: Rabies virus (a negative-sense, bullet-shaped rhabdovirus) is transmitted through the bite or scratch of an infected rabid animal (e.g., dog, bat), inoculating viral saliva into deep dermal tissues and skeletal muscle.
  • Primary Replication: Following entry, the virus undergoes an initial period of local replication within skeletal muscle fibers and local connective tissues at the inoculation site. This local amplification stage corresponds to the highly variable incubation period.
  • Neuroinvasion: Once sufficient viral particles accumulate, the viral glycoprotein binds to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChR) or NCAM at the neuromuscular junction, entering motor nerve endings to travel centripetally via retrograde fast axonal transport ($50\text{--}100\text{ mm/day}$) to the dorsal root ganglia and the central nervous system (brain), culminating in fatal encephalomyelitis.

question: Route of entry for canine distemper virus is
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Route of Entry for Canine Distemper Virus (CDV):
  • Canine Distemper Virus (CDV): A highly contagious, enveloped negative-sense single-stranded RNA virus belonging to the genus Morbillivirus (family Paramyxoviridae), closely related to human measles virus.
  • Transmission and Route of Entry: Transmission occurs predominantly via inhaled aerosolized droplets or direct contact with respiratory secretions from infected animals.
  • The virus initially infects respiratory epithelial cells and resident alveolar/macrophage dendritic cells in the upper respiratory tract. Following local replication, it rapidly disseminates to regional bronchial lymph nodes and systemic lymphoid tissues, producing profound lymphopenia and subsequent multi-organ disease (catarrhal, gastrointestinal, and severe neurological signs).

question: Callipyge gene mutation in sheep leads to increased muscle growth. The gene presents a typical case of Polar over-dominance. Which of the four genotypes given below shows increased muscle growth? (N= wild type allele, C= mutant allele for callipyge)
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Polar Over-Dominance in the Callipyge Sheep Phenotype:
  • Callipyge ($CLPG$): A famous mutation located in an imprinted gene cluster on sheep chromosome 18 that causes severe muscular hypertrophy (double muscling) localized primarily to the pelvic limbs and loin.
  • Polar Over-Dominance: A unique, non-Mendelian parent-of-origin inheritance mode where:
    • $N^{\text{mat}} C^{\text{pat}}$ (Maternal normal $N$, Paternal mutant $C$): The ONLY genotype that expresses the callipyge muscular hypertrophy phenotype!
    • $N^{\text{mat}} N^{\text{pat}}$ (Wild-type): Normal muscling.
    • $C^{\text{mat}} N^{\text{pat}}$ (Maternal mutant $C$, Paternal normal $N$): Normal muscling.
    • $C^{\text{mat}} C^{\text{pat}}$ (Homozygous mutant): Normal muscling (the callipyge phenotype is mysteriously silenced in homozygotes due to complex trans-interaction of maternal non-coding RNAs like Gtl2 with paternal retrotransposon-like gene Peg11/Rtl1).
  • Thus, only the heterozygous genotype with the mutant allele inherited from the father ($N^{\text{mat}} C^{\text{pat}}$) shows increased muscle growth.

question: The technique used in animal biotechnology for the rapid multiplication and production of animals with a desirable genotype is:
options: in vitro fertilization and embryo transfer
correct_answer: in vitro fertilization and embryo transfer
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Reproductive Technologies for Animal Multiplication:
  • IVF and Embryo Transfer (IVF-ET): In animal biotechnology, multiple ovulation and embryo transfer (MOET) combined with in vitro fertilization (IVF) is the primary reproductive biotechnology utilized for the rapid multiplication and elite genetic propagation of farm livestock (cattle, sheep, horses).
  • Oocytes harvested from genetically superior females (donors) are fertilized in vitro with high-value semen and cultured to the blastocyst stage before non-surgical transfer into synchronized recipient surrogate mothers. This allows a single genetically prized female to produce dozens of offspring per year instead of just one.
  • Protoplast fusion is a plant biotechnology technique inapplicable to animal cells; artificial insemination multiplies male genetics only, not whole genotypes.

question: A primary culture of neurons isolated from the mouse brain responded positively when exposed to a chemical for a few seconds, but the neurons were less responsive and eventually stopped responding when exposed to the same chemical for prolonged duration. However, if the culture was left for some time and washed, the neurons started responding to the same chemical at the same concentration as before. The reduced response was due to
options: change in the pH of the medium.
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Receptor Desensitization and Down-Regulation:
  • Tachyphylaxis / Desensitization: When cell-surface receptors (such as GPCRs or ligand-gated ion channels) are exposed to a chemical agonist for prolonged periods, the cellular response rapidly wanes despite the continuous presence of the ligand.
  • Molecular Mechanism:
    • Within seconds to minutes, active receptors are phosphorylated by G-protein coupled receptor kinases (GRKs) or second-messenger kinases (PKA/PKC), recruiting $\beta$-arrestin, which sterically uncouples the receptor from its G-protein (homologous desensitization).
    • With extended exposure, $\beta$-arrestin targets the receptors to clathrin-coated pits for endocytic internalization (receptor down-regulation).
  • When the agonist is washed away and cells are rested, internalized receptors are dephosphorylated by endosomal phosphatases and recycled back to the plasma membrane, fully restoring receptor responsiveness to subsequent challenges.

question: If a neuron is tyrosine hydroxylase positive, it could be either:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Biosynthetic Pathway of Catecholamine Neurotransmitters:
  • Tyrosine Hydroxylase (TH): The initial and rate-limiting enzyme in the biosynthesis of all catecholamines. It catalyzes the addition of a hydroxyl group to the aromatic ring of L-tyrosine: $$\text{L-Tyrosine} \xrightarrow{\text{Tyrosine Hydroxylase}} \text{L-DOPA}$$
  • Subsequent Conversions:
    • $\text{L-DOPA} \xrightarrow{\text{Aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase}} \mathbf{\text{Dopamine}}$ (present in dopaminergic neurons).
    • $\text{Dopamine} \xrightarrow{\text{Dopamine } \beta\text{-hydroxylase}} \mathbf{\text{Norepinephrine}}$ (present in noradrenergic neurons).
  • Serotonergic neurons synthesize serotonin from tryptophan using tryptophan hydroxylase (not TH); histaminergic neurons synthesize histamine from histidine using histidine decarboxylase.
  • Therefore, a tyrosine hydroxylase-positive neuron is either Noradrenergic or Dopaminergic.

question: Pain sensation is a subjective and conscious feeling. However, although the autonomic organs viz. brain, heart etc. do not get represented in the cerebral cortex, one feels pain in those parts as well. The reason is
options: these parts receive less blood supply.
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Neurobiology of Referred Pain:
  • Referred Pain: The clinical phenomenon where visceral nociceptive pain originating from deep internal autonomic organs (such as the heart during myocardial ischemia or the gallbladder) is perceived as originating from distant superficial somatic structures (such as the skin of the left chest wall, neck, and inner left arm).
  • Convergence-Projection Theory: Autonomic visceral nociceptive afferent nerve fibers and somatic cutaneous sensory afferent fibers converge onto and synapse with the exact same second-order projection spinothalamic neurons in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord (e.g., spinal segments T1–T5 for cardiac and somatic arm fibers).
  • Because the sensory cerebral cortex has far greater somatotopic representation for body surface areas than for internal organs, higher cortical centers misinterpret the incoming impulses as originating from the somatic dermatome rather than the visceral organ.

question: Neurons are formed from precursor proneural cells due to
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Delta-Notch Lateral Inhibition and Proneural Cell Specification:
  • During neurogenesis in Drosophila and vertebrates, a cluster of equipotent ectodermal cells in a proneural cluster has the potential to become neurons.
  • Lateral Inhibition Cascade:
    • Stochastic upregulation of proneural basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) transcription factors (like Achaete-Scute) in one cell causes it to express high levels of the cell-surface ligand Delta.
    • Delta binds to the Notch receptor on neighboring surrounding cells, triggering proteolytic cleavage of Notch by presenilin/$\gamma$-secretase. The intracellular domain of Notch ($NICD$) translocates to the nucleus to activate repressor genes (such as Hairy and Enhancer of Split, $Hes$), which repress proneural genes, forcing those neighbors to adopt an epidermal/glial fate.
  • Meanwhile, the central cell that successfully differentiates into a mature neuron maintains low Notch activity and escapes lateral inhibition.

question: A neuron at resting state when treated with “X” showed transmembrane potential -50mV, while when treated with “Y” it showed -90mV. Given such a condition, which of the following statements would be most appropriate?
options: The threshold for inducing a response by the neuron was higher for “X” than that for “Y”.
Both the treatments induced depolarization of the neuron.
Both the treatments induced hyperpolarization of the neuron.
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Electrophysiological Definitions: Depolarization vs. Hyperpolarization:
  • Resting Membrane Potential ($V_m$): In typical neurons, the resting membrane potential is negative, around $-70\text{ mV}$.
  • Treatment X ($V_m = -50\text{ mV}$): The membrane potential becomes less negative (moves from $-70\text{ mV}$ towards $0\text{ mV}$). A shift towards a less negative/more positive potential is defined as depolarization (often caused by influx of $\text{Na}^+$ or $\text{Ca}^{2+}$).
  • Treatment Y ($V_m = -90\text{ mV}$): The membrane potential becomes more negative than resting potential (moves from $-70\text{ mV}$ down to $-90\text{ mV}$). A shift towards a more negative potential is defined as hyperpolarization (often caused by efflux of $\text{K}^+$ or influx of $\text{Cl}^-$).
  • Therefore, “X” induced depolarization, while “Y” induced hyperpolarization.

question: In a population which is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, the frequency of a recessive allele for a certain genetic trait is 0.40. What percentage of individuals would be expected to show the dominant trait in the next generation?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium Trait Frequency Calculation:
  • Given:
    • Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium holds ($p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1$).
    • Frequency of the recessive allele: $q = 0.40$.
  • Step 1: Calculate dominant allele frequency ($p$): $$p + q = 1 \implies p = 1 - 0.40 = 0.60$$
  • Step 2: Calculate percentage of individuals showing the dominant trait: Individuals displaying the dominant phenotype include both homozygous dominant ($AA$) and heterozygous ($Aa$) genotypes: $$\text{Frequency of dominant trait} = p^2 + 2pq = 1 - q^2$$ $$\text{Frequency} = 1 - (0.40)^2 = 1 - 0.16 = 0.84 = \mathbf{84\%}$$
  • Alternatively: $$p^2 = (0.60)^2 = 0.36 \quad (36\%)$$ $$2pq = 2(0.60)(0.40) = 0.48 \quad (48\%)$$ $$\text{Total dominant phenotype} = 36\% + 48\% = \mathbf{84\%}$$

question: Color blindness in human is a sex-linked recessive trait. If two individuals with normal color vision have a color blind son, what will be the genotypes of the parents?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Genetics of X-Linked Recessive Inheritance (Color Blindness):
  • Trait: Red-green color blindness is an $X$-linked recessive condition ($X^c$ = mutant allele, $X^C$ = wild-type normal vision allele).
  • Child's Genotype: The affected son has the hemizygous genotype $X^c Y$.
    • He must inherit the $Y$ chromosome from his father.
    • He must inherit the mutant $X^c$ chromosome from his mother.
  • Parents' Genotypes:
    • Father has normal color vision, so he carries a normal $X$ chromosome: $X^C Y$.
    • Mother has normal color vision, but must have contributed the $X^c$ allele to her son; therefore, she must be a phenotypically normal heterozygous carrier: $X^C X^c$.
  • Therefore, the parental genotypes are $X^C X^c$ and $X^C Y$.

question: A human is phenotypically female, but her interphase somatic nuclei do not display the existence of Barr bodies. Which of the following conditions could explain the above feature?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Lyon Hypothesis, Barr Bodies, and Sex Chromosome Aneuploidies:
  • Lyonization and Barr Body Rule: In mammalian somatic cells, dosage compensation occurs by random transcriptional inactivation of all $X$ chromosomes in excess of one. The number of visible heterochromatic Barr bodies formed at interphase equals: $$\mathbf{\text{Number of Barr Bodies} = N_X - 1}$$ where $N_X$ is the total number of $X$ chromosomes in the karyotype.
  • Evaluation of Conditions:
    • Normal Female ($46,XX$): $2 - 1 = 1$ Barr body.
    • Klinefelter Syndrome ($47,XXY$): $2 - 1 = 1$ Barr body (phenotypically male).
    • Triple X Syndrome ($47,XXX$): $3 - 1 = 2$ Barr bodies.
    • Turner Syndrome ($45,X0$): Possesses only a single $X$ chromosome ($N_X = 1$). Therefore, number of Barr bodies $= 1 - 1 = \mathbf{0}$! Individuals are phenotypically female with short stature, gonadal dysgenesis, and somatic nuclei lacking Barr bodies.

question: For the pedigree depicted below, which mode(s) of inheritance CANNOT be possible?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Pedigree Analysis Rules of Exclusion:
  • Rules for X-Linked Recessive Inheritance:
    1. An affected female must be homozygous ($X^r X^r$). She must inherit one $X^r$ from her mother and one $X^r$ from her father. Therefore, an affected female must have an affected father ($X^r Y$).
    2. All sons of an affected female must inherit her mutant $X^r$ chromosome. Therefore, an affected mother must produce 100% affected sons.
  • If a pedigree shows an unaffected father having an affected daughter, or an affected mother having an unaffected son, X-linked recessive inheritance is strictly impossible (CANNOT be possible).

question: C banding of human chromosomes specifically reveals
options: polymorphism of constitutive heterochromatin of chromosomes 1, 9, 16 and Y
polymorphism of constitutive heterochromatin of chromosomes 3, 7, 12 and X
polymorphism of facultative heterochromatin of chromosome X
correct_answer: polymorphism of constitutive heterochromatin of chromosomes 1, 9, 16 and Y
explanation:
[CONCEPT] C-Banding of Human Metaphase Chromosomes:
  • C-Banding (Constitutive Heterochromatin Banding): Involves treating metaphase chromosome spreads with barium hydroxide [$\text{Ba(OH)}_2$] at elevated temperatures followed by Giemsa staining.
  • This alkaline denaturing treatment selectively extracts DNA from euchromatin while leaving highly condensed, transcriptionally inactive constitutive heterochromatin intact at centromeric regions.
  • In humans, C-banding reveals marked length and structural polymorphisms in the large pericentromeric blocks of constitutive heterochromatin located on chromosomes 1, 9, 16, and the distal long arm of the Y chromosome ($Yq$).

question: Which one of the following expressions is likely to retrieve more matches in a database search?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Regular Expression Matching and Degeneracy in Sequence Databases:
  • In pattern matching (e.g., PROSITE motif syntax):
    • Square brackets $[\dots]$ denote allowable amino acid alternatives at that position.
    • $'X'$ represents a complete wildcard matching any of the 20 standard amino acids.
  • Evaluating Retrieval Diversity:
    • D-A-V-I-D: Matches only $1 \times 1 \times 1 \times 1 \times 1 = 1$ unique 5-mer sequence.
    • [DE]-A-V-I-[DE]: Matches $2 \times 1 \times 1 \times 1 \times 2 = 4$ unique 5-mer sequences.
    • D-A-V-E: Matches only $1$ unique 4-mer sequence.
    • [DE]-[AVILM]-X-E: Matches $2 \text{ (D or E)} \times 5 \text{ (A, V, I, L, or M)} \times 20 \text{ (any amino acid for X)} \times 1 \text{ (E)} = \mathbf{200}$ distinct peptide sequence variants!
  • Because it defines 200 possible matches, [DE]-[AVILM]-X-E is statistically guaranteed to retrieve vastly more matches in a sequence database.

question: Which substitution matrices should you prefer to find distantly related orthologs through BLAST search?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Selection of Substitution Scoring Matrices in BLAST:
  • BLOSUM Matrices (Henikoff & Henikoff): Derived from local multiple alignments of conserved protein blocks. The numerical index represents the minimum percent sequence identity of clustered sequences:
    • Higher BLOSUM numbers (e.g., BLOSUM 80, 90): Tailored for closely related sequences ($>80\%$ identity).
    • Lower BLOSUM numbers (e.g., BLOSUM 45, BLOSUM 40): Tailored for distantly related sequences / distant orthologs ($<45\%$ identity).
  • PAM Matrices (Dayhoff): Based on Point Accepted Mutations per 100 amino acids:
    • Lower PAM numbers (e.g., PAM 30, PAM 120): Tailored for closely related homologs.
    • Higher PAM numbers (e.g., PAM 250): Represents 250 evolutionary changes per 100 residues, tailored for distantly related homologs.
  • Therefore, to detect distant orthologs, one should choose BLOSUM 40 and PAM 250.

question: Match the items in Group 1 with an appropriate description in Group 2 Group I Group 2 P. UPGMA 1. Protein sequence database Q. CLUSTALW 2. Phylogenetic Analysis R. SWISS-PROT 3. 3-D structure visualization S. RasMol 4. Multiple sequence alignment
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Bioinformatics Tools and Databases Matching:
  • P. UPGMA $\to$ 2. Phylogenetic Analysis: Unweighted Pair Group Method with Arithmetic Mean; a hierarchical distance-based clustering algorithm used to construct phenograms and phylogenetic trees.
  • Q. CLUSTALW $\to$ 4. Multiple Sequence Alignment: A widely utilized progressive multiple sequence alignment program for DNA and protein sequences.
  • R. SWISS-PROT $\to$ 1. Protein Sequence Database: A manually curated, non-redundant, high-quality protein sequence database maintained by UniProt.
  • S. RasMol $\to$ 3. 3-D Structure Visualization: A classic standalone molecular graphics software program utilized for interactive 3-D visualization of macromolecular crystal structures (PDB files).
  • Correct match: P-2, Q-4, R-1, S-3.

question: The rate of substitutions in a certain region of DNA of length 1000 bases is estimated as 10-9 per base per year. If two species diverged approximately 10 million years ago, the fraction of sites that differ between them should be approximately
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Molecular Clock and Sequence Divergence Calculation:
  • Given:
    • Length of DNA region ($L$) = $1000\text{ bases}$
    • Rate of substitution ($r$) = $10^{-9}\text{ substitutions/base/year}$
    • Divergence time from common ancestor ($T$) = $10\text{ million years} = 10^7\text{ years}$
  • Total Divergence Time: Because both lineages evolve independently and accumulate mutations after diverging from their most recent common ancestor, the total evolutionary time separating the two modern species is: $$T_{\text{total}} = 2 \times T = 2 \times 10^7\text{ years}$$
  • Fraction of Differing Sites ($K$): $$K = 2 \cdot r \cdot T = 2 \times 10^{-9} \times 10^7 = 2 \times 10^{-2} = \mathbf{0.02 = 2\%}$$
  • Therefore, approximately 2% of the nucleotide sites will differ between the two species.

question: When searching the Blocks and PRINTS databases, a match is judged significant if
options: a combined E-value above a given threshold is reported for a multiple -motif match
correct_answer: a combined E-value above a given threshold is reported for a multiple -motif match
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Significance Criteria in Blocks and PRINTS Databases:
  • PRINTS and BLOCKS: Secondary protein family databases based on fingerprints—conserved, ungapped motifs that characterize sub-regions of a protein family fold.
  • A single motif might match fortuitously by random chance. However, a true member of the family must match multiple conserved motifs in the correct sequential order with appropriate spacing.
  • To determine statistical significance, the search algorithm evaluates all motif hits across the query sequence and calculates a combined E-value (or combined score) across the multiple motifs. A match is deemed statistically significant if this composite multiple-motif score meets the significance threshold.

question: Two species are found to share a cluster of 8 genes, but the genes are in different orders in the two species. The orders are represented by signed permutations as given below: Species X 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8 Species Y 1, 2,-5,-4,-3,8,6,7 The transformation between the two gene orders
options: cannot be achieved by inversions alone.
can be achieved by one translocation and one inversion.
can be achieved by three inversions.
requires six separate genome rearrangement events.
correct_answer: can be achieved by one translocation and one inversion.
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Genome Rearrangements by Inversions and Translocations:
  • Species X Gene Order: $1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8$
  • Species Y Gene Order: $1, 2, -5, -4, -3, 8, 6, 7$
  • Step-by-Step Transformation:
    1. Inversion: Invert the segment $(3, 4, 5)$. Reversing both order and strand orientation yields $(-5, -4, -3)$: $$1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 \xrightarrow{\text{Inversion of }(3,4,5)} 1, 2, -5, -4, -3, 6, 7, 8$$
    2. Translocation / Transposition: Translocate gene $8$ from the distal position to an internal position between $-3$ and $6$: $$1, 2, -5, -4, -3, 6, 7, 8 \xrightarrow{\text{Translocation of } 8} 1, 2, -5, -4, -3, 8, 6, 7$$
  • Thus, the transformation between the two gene orders can be achieved by one inversion and one translocation.

question: As the E value of a BLAST search becomes smaller
options: the value K also becomes smaller
the score tends to be larger
the probability p tends to be larger
the extreme value distribution becomes less skewed
correct_answer: the score tends to be larger
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Karlin-Altschul Statistics and BLAST E-Values:
  • In pairwise local sequence alignment algorithms (BLAST), the statistical significance of a high-scoring segment pair (HSP) with raw score $S$ is evaluated using Karlin-Altschul extreme value distribution statistics: $$\mathbf{E = K \cdot m \cdot n \cdot e^{-\lambda S}}$$ where $m$ and $n$ are the lengths of the query and database, and $K$ and $\lambda$ are natural scale parameters.
  • Relationship Between Score and E-Value: Because the score $S$ appears in a negative exponential term ($-e^{-\lambda S}$): $$\text{As alignment score } S \text{ increases} \implies e^{-\lambda S} \text{ drops exponentially} \implies E \text{ becomes smaller!}$$
  • Therefore, as the $E$-value becomes smaller (more statistically significant, less likely to be a random chance match), the alignment score tends to be larger.

question: In a genome with average GC-content 40%, the expected frequency of occurrence of the tetranucleotide AACG is
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Expected Frequency of Oligonucleotides from Base Composition:
  • Given: Average genomic GC-content = $40\% = 0.40$.
  • By Chargaff's parity rules: $$f(G) = f(C) = \frac{0.40}{2} = 0.20$$ $$f(A) = f(T) = \frac{1 - 0.40}{2} = \frac{0.60}{2} = 0.30$$
  • Probability of Tetranucleotide AACG: Assuming a random independent multinomial distribution of nucleotides: $$P(\text{AACG}) = f(A) \times f(A) \times f(C) \times f(G)$$ $$P(\text{AACG}) = (0.30) \times (0.30) \times (0.20) \times (0.20)$$ $$P(\text{AACG}) = 0.09 \times 0.04 = 0.0036$$
  • Converting to percentage: $$\text{Percentage} = 0.0036 \times 100\% = \mathbf{0.36\%}$$

question: Consider that you have collected X-ray diffraction data on three different protein crystals, referred to as Protein A, B and C. Data set for crystal A has the best diffraction spot at 8A, crystal B at 5A and crystal C has the best diffraction at 3A. Which data set is likely to yield a higher resolution crystal structure?
options: All will have same resolution structure
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Resolution in Macromolecular X-Ray Crystallography:
