  • Bragg's Law of X-Ray Diffraction: $$\lambda = 2d \sin\theta \implies d = \frac{\lambda}{2\sin\theta}$$
  • Physical Meaning of $d$-Spacing:
    • $d$ represents the minimum interplanar spacing of crystal lattice planes that produce observable diffraction spots.
    • Diffraction spots observed at higher scattering angles ($2\theta$) correspond to smaller $d$-spacings.
    • A smaller numerical value of $d$ represents higher spatial resolution (the ability to resolve two atomic centers that are closer together).
  • Comparing the three crystals:
    • Crystal A: $8\text{ \AA}$ (Low resolution, only shows overall molecular envelope).
    • Crystal B: $5\text{ \AA}$ (Medium-low resolution, shows secondary structure cylinders).
    • Crystal C: $3\text{ \AA}$ (High resolution, allows tracing of the polypeptide backbone and side chains).
  • Therefore, Crystal C yields the highest resolution structure.

question: In a protein crystallization experiment, you have identified an optimal protein concentration and precipitant concentration which yield crystals. Now if you are asked to grow crystals again with a protein solution that is four times more concentrated, how will you alter the precipitant concentration? Ans. B Ans.C Please visit.... www.easybiologyclass.com www.easybiologyclass.com
options: Keep the precipitant concertation the same
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Phase Diagrams and Optimization in Protein Crystallization:
  • Protein crystallization is governed by phase solubility diagrams plotting protein concentration versus precipitant (e.g., PEG, ammonium sulfate) concentration: $$\text{Undersaturated} \longrightarrow \text{Metastable (Crystal Growth)} \longrightarrow \text{Labile (Spontaneous Nucleation)} \longrightarrow \text{Precipitation}$$
  • Effect of Increasing Protein Concentration: If the protein concentration is increased 4-fold, the solution shifts deeply into the excessive supersaturation/precipitation zone where disordered, amorphous precipitation or massive microcrystalline showers occur.
  • To keep the system balanced inside the optimal metastable nucleation zone for growing large, well-ordered single crystals, one must decrease the precipitant concentration.

question: Which of the following statements is true for two different tripeptides consisting of either glycine or proline?
options: Glycine tripeptide will have relatively larger allowed area on the Ramachandran plot.
Proline tripeptide will have relatively larger allowed area on the Ramachandran plot.
Both the tripeptides will fall primarily in the disallowed regions of the Ramachandran plot.
Both the tripeptides will fall primarily in the overlapping allowed regions of the Ramachandran plot.
correct_answer: Glycine tripeptide will have relatively larger allowed area on the Ramachandran plot.
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Ramachandran Plot Conformational Flexibility of Glycine vs. Proline:
  • Ramachandran Plot: Visualizes energetically allowed torsional dihedral angles $\phi$ ($C_\alpha - N$) and $\psi$ ($C_\alpha - C$) for amino acid residues in a polypeptide backbone.
  • Glycine ($-\text{H}$ side chain): Glycine lacks a $\beta$-carbon and has only a single hydrogen atom as its side chain. Steric clashes between the side chain and backbone atoms are virtually non-existent, permitting glycine to explore all four quadrants of the plot (occupying $\sim 61\%$ of conformational space).
  • Proline (Pyrrolidine ring): Proline has its side chain cyclized back onto its own amino nitrogen, locking its $\phi$ angle rigidly near $-65^\circ \pm 15^\circ$ and drastically limiting allowed $\psi$ angles.
  • Therefore, a Glycine tripeptide will have a relatively much larger allowed area on the Ramachandran plot.

question: In a Fluorescence Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET) experiment, the donor is Cyan Fluorescent Protein (CFP) which has excitation and emission maxima at 435 and 485 nm, respectively. The acceptor in this experiment is Yellow Fluorescent Protein (YFP) that has excitation and emission maxima at 513 and 545 nm, respectively . Under the conditions, where a significant FRET is observed, what will happen to the FRET signal if the emission maxima of CFP is made to shift to 475nm.
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Fluorescence Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET) and Spectral Overlap:
  • Förster Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET): Non-radiative dipole-dipole energy transfer from an excited donor fluorophore to a ground-state acceptor fluorophore.
  • FRET Efficiency Formula: $$E = \frac{R_0^6}{R_0^6 + r^6}$$ where Förster distance $R_0$ depends directly on the spectral overlap integral $J(\lambda)$ between the donor's normalized fluorescence emission spectrum and the acceptor's molar absorption spectrum: $$J(\lambda) = \int f_D(\lambda) \, \varepsilon_A(\lambda) \, \lambda^4 \, d\lambda$$
  • Effect of Shifting CFP Emission: Acceptor YFP absorbs maximally at $513\text{ nm}$. If the CFP donor emission maximum shifts from $485\text{ nm}$ down to $475\text{ nm}$, its emission spectrum moves further away from YFP's absorption band, significantly reducing the spectral overlap integral $J(\lambda)$. Consequently, the FRET signal will decrease.

question: Consider that the following polypeptides are being analyzed by Mass- spectrometry (MS). These peptides are generated by proteolytic cleavage of a protein that is expressed in mammalian cells and it has undergone glycosylation, phosphorylation and acetylation. What will the expected positioning of the spectra corresponding to these peptides (smaller to larger)?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Mass Spectrometry Profiling of Modified Peptides:
  • In tandem mass spectrometry (MS), peptides are separated by their mass-to-charge ratio ($m/z$). Post-translational modifications (PTMs) introduce distinct mass additions:
    • Phosphorylation: $+80\text{ Da}$ (addition of $\text{HPO}_3$).
    • Acetylation: $+42\text{ Da}$ (addition of $\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\text{O}$).
    • $N$-linked or $O$-linked Glycosylation: Hundreds to thousands of Daltons.
  • Depending on residue target motifs (e.g. Asn in consensus $N$-glycosylation motifs $\text{Asn-X-Ser/Thr}$), peptides acquire differential mass shifts, yielding an ordered spectrum from smaller to larger molecular weights.

question: Assuming that the sequence of CDRs of an antibody are heavily enriched with Tyrosine and Serine, what is likely to be the driving force stabilizing its interaction with the antigen?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Complementarity-Determining Regions (CDRs) and Antigen-Antibody Binding:
  • CDRs (Hypervariable Loops): The antigen-binding site (paratope) of an antibody is shaped by six CDR loops (three on the light chain and three on the heavy chain).
  • Role of Tyrosine and Serine:
    • Tyrosine contains a planar aromatic ring and a polar phenolic hydroxyl ($-\text{OH}$) group.
    • Serine possesses a primary aliphatic hydroxyl ($-\text{OH}$) group.
  • Hydroxyl groups are exceptionally versatile hydrogen-bonding partners, functioning simultaneously as excellent hydrogen-bond donors and hydrogen-bond acceptors. When antibody CDRs are heavily enriched in Tyr and Ser, their paratopes stabilize antigen interactions predominantly through extensive networks of hydrogen bonding (supplemented by aromatic stacking).

question: Hydrophobic amino acids are prevalent in transmembrane regions of membrane embedded proteins because
options: Hydrophobic amino acids destabilize the membrane bilayer and increase membrane fluidity
Phospholipid tails are hydrophobic and therefore membrane embedded regions can be stabilized through hydrophobic interactions
The side chains of hydrophobic amino acids interact covalently with phospholipids
It is just a random occurrence originated from heavy bias of hydrophobic amino acids in protein sequences
correct_answer: Phospholipid tails are hydrophobic and therefore membrane embedded regions can be stabilized through hydrophobic interactions
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Thermodynamic Stability of Transmembrane Protein Domains:
  • Membrane Architecture: Biological lipid bilayers consist of hydrophilic zwitterionic polar headgroups facing the aqueous environment and an interior hydrophobic core consisting of long hydrocarbon fatty acid acyl chains ($16\text{--}18$ carbons).
  • Transmembrane Domains: The segments of integral membrane proteins spanning the lipid bilayer are almost universally structured as $\alpha$-helices rich in non-polar, hydrophobic amino acids (such as Leucine, Isoleucine, Valine, Phenylalanine, and Alanine).
  • The non-polar side chains project outward and establish favorable hydrophobic interactions and van der Waals contacts with the nonpolar fatty acyl tails of phospholipids, avoiding the enormous thermodynamic penalty of exposing hydrophobic side chains to water.

question: Bryostatin is an anticancer agent obtained from:
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Marine Natural Products: Bryostatin from Bugula neritina:
  • Bryostatin 1: A complex macrocyclic lactone (polyketide) with potent antineoplastic, neuroprotective, and memory-enhancing activities that acts as a high-affinity modulator of protein kinase C (PKC).
  • Source Organism: Bryostatin was originally isolated from the marine colonial bryozoan (moss animal) Bugula neritina.
  • Subsequent molecular metagenomic investigations revealed that bryostatins are actually synthesized by the bryozoan's obligate uncultured bacterial endosymbiont, Candidatus Endobugula sertula.

question: Synthesis of White spot syndrome virus envelop takes place in
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Replication and Assembly of White Spot Syndrome Virus (WSSV):
  • White Spot Syndrome Virus (WSSV): A major lethal viral pathogen of cultured marine penaeid shrimp (such as Penaeus monodon), belonging to the family Nimaviridae (genus Whispovirus). It possesses a huge circular double-stranded DNA genome ($>300\text{ kb}$).
  • Nuclear Envelopment: Most enveloped animal viruses acquire their lipid envelopes by budding through host cellular membranes (ER, Golgi, or plasma membrane). Uniquely, WSSV virions assemble their rod-shaped nucleocapsids and acquire their trilaminar lipid envelope de novo directly inside the hypertrophied nucleus of infected host cells!

question: Primary etiology of Epizootic Ulcerative Syndrome is a Fungus Aphanomyces invadans. Its zoospores have the property to
options: travel long distances and penetrate deep in to the tissue
correct_answer: travel long distances and penetrate deep in to the tissue
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Etiology and Pathogenesis of Epizootic Ulcerative Syndrome (EUS):
  • Epizootic Ulcerative Syndrome (EUS) / Red Spot Disease: A devastating, seasonal epizootic disease of wild and farmed freshwater and estuarine fish caused by the invasive water mold Aphanomyces invadans (an oomycete).
  • Zoospores: The infectious units are motile, biflagellate secondary zoospores. Upon attaching to damaged fish skin, zoospores encyst and germinate, producing specialized invasive hyphae that have the unique capacity to penetrate deeply into dermal muscle layers, traveling deep into visceral tissues.
  • This deep invasive hyphal growth elicits severe chronic granulomatous inflammation, causing extensive muscular liquefactive necrosis and massive crater-like skin ulcers.

question: Gonad Inhibiting Hormone (GIH) in crustaceans is synthesized in
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Endocrine Regulation in Crustaceans (The X-Organ / Sinus Gland Complex):
  • In decapod crustaceans (lobsters, crabs, prawns), neuroendocrine control is centered in the eyestalk neurosecretory complex:
    • The X-Organ (Medulla Terminalis Ganglionic X-Organ, MTGXO): A cluster of neurosecretory cell bodies located in the optic ganglia of the eyestalk. It synthesizes peptide hormones of the CHH family, including Gonad-Inhibiting Hormone (GIH, also known as Vitellogenesis-Inhibiting Hormone, VIH) and Moult-Inhibiting Hormone (MIH).
    • The Sinus Gland: A neurohemal storage and release organ where axon terminals of the X-organ store and release hormones into the hemolymph.
    • The Y-Organ: An epithelial endocrine gland in the head that secretes ecdysteroids (moulting hormone).
  • Therefore, Gonad Inhibiting Hormone is synthesized in the X-organ.

question: The synthetic equivalent of neuro-pharmacologically active peptides obtained from the marine snail Conus magus is
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Marine Conopeptides and Ziconotide (Prialt):
  • Conotoxins: Marine predatory cone snails (genus Conus) produce complex cocktails of small, disulfide-rich neurotoxic venom peptides used to paralyze prey fish rapidly.
  • Conus magus (Magician's Cone): Secretes $\omega$-conotoxin MVIIA, a 25-amino-acid peptide with three disulfide bridges that selectively and reversibly blocks neuronal N-type voltage-sensitive calcium channels ($Ca_v2.2$) in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord.
  • Ziconotide (Prialt): The synthetic equivalent of $\omega$-conotoxin MVIIA, approved by the US FDA as an intrathecal non-opioid analgesic for managing intractable, severe chronic neuropathic pain (over 1000 times more potent than morphine without causing drug tolerance).

question: Viral encephalopathy and retinopathy in fishes are caused by
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Viral Encephalopathy and Retinopathy (VER) in Marine Fishes:
  • Viral Encephalopathy and Retinopathy (VER): Also known as Viral Nervous Necrosis (VNN), this is one of the most destructive infectious viral diseases affecting larval, juvenile, and adult marine fishes (sea bass, grouper, halibut) worldwide.
  • Etiologic Agent: Caused by Betanodavirus, a non-enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded bisegmented RNA virus belonging to the family Nodaviridae.
  • The virus targets the central nervous system and retina, causing extensive cellular vacuolation, necrosis, and abnormal swimming behavior (spinning and whirling).

question: A pigment isolated from marine red algae that finds application in flow cytometry is
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Phycobiliproteins as Fluorescent Probes in Flow Cytometry:
  • Phycoerythrin (PE / R-Phycoerythrin): A brilliant red-fluorescing phycobiliprotein isolated from marine red algae (such as Porphyridium cruentum or Gastroclonium).
  • Photophysical Properties:
    • Extremely high molar extinction coefficient ($\varepsilon \approx 1.96 \times 10^6\text{ M}^{-1}\cdot\text{cm}^{-1}$).
    • High fluorescence quantum yield ($\Phi \approx 0.82$).
    • Excitation peak matching standard argon/solid-state lasers ($488\text{ nm}$ or $532\text{ nm}$) with emission in the orange-yellow band ($\sim 575\text{ nm}$).
  • Its extraordinary brightness makes phycoerythrin one of the most widely used fluorochromes conjugated to monoclonal antibodies for immunophenotyping in flow cytometry.

question: Which of the following electron acceptor that is used by the bacteria is mainly responsible for marine corrosion?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Microbiologically Influenced Corrosion (MIC) in Marine Environments:
  • Sulfate-Reducing Bacteria (SRB): In marine biofilms and anoxic sediments, sulfate-reducing bacteria (such as Desulfovibrio and Desulfotomaculum) are the primary culprits causing severe microbiologically influenced corrosion (MIC) of steel pipelines, ships, and offshore rigs.
  • Respiration Mechanism: Seawater contains a high concentration of sulfate ions ($\sim 28\text{ mM}$). Under anaerobic conditions, SRB use sulfate ($\text{SO}_4^{2-}$) as their terminal electron acceptor to oxidize organic acids or molecular hydrogen: $$\text{SO}_4^{2-} + 4\text{H}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{SRB}} \text{S}^{2-} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
  • The generated sulfide reacts with iron to form cathodic iron sulfides ($FeS$) and depolarizes hydrogen at the metal surface, triggering rapid localized pitting corrosion and structural failure.

question: Which one of the following bacterial species is responsible for the Scombroid fish poisoning? Ans. A Ans. B Please visit.... www.easybiologyclass.com www.easybiologyclass.com
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Microbiology of Scombroid (Histamine) Fish Poisoning:
  • Scombroid Poisoning: A food intoxication resulting from eating spoiled scombroid fish (tuna, mackerel, bonito) that contain high levels of free L-histidine in their dark muscle tissue.
  • Bacterial Histidine Decarboxylation: When fish are not immediately chilled, psychrotrophic and mesophilic bacteria possessing the enzyme histidine decarboxylase convert histidine into toxic histamine: $$\text{L-Histidine} \xrightarrow{\text{Histidine decarboxylase}} \text{Histamine} + \text{CO}_2$$
  • Marine psychrotolerant species such as Photobacterium phosphoreum (along with Morganella morganii) are key prolific histamine producers capable of generating toxic levels of histamine even during cold storage.

question: The larval stage of Macrobrachium rosenbergii is referred to as
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Larval Development of the Giant Freshwater Prawn (Macrobrachium rosenbergii):
  • The giant freshwater prawn Macrobrachium rosenbergii is a catadromous crustacean; adult females migrate to brackish estuarine water to hatch their eggs.
  • Larval Stages: The eggs hatch directly into free-swimming, planktonic, phototactic larvae that pass through 11 distinct larval stages (spanning roughly $20\text{--}35\text{ days}$) characterized by zoeal and mysis-like morphology before undergoing metamorphosis into benthic post-larvae (PL).

question: The group of marine algae which have urea cycle is
explanation:
[CONCEPT] The Ornithine-Urea Cycle (OUC) in Marine Diatoms:
  • In animal physiology, the urea cycle functions to detoxify ammonia into urea for excretion.
  • Discovery in Diatoms: Genomic sequencing of the model marine diatoms Thalassiosira pseudonana and Phaeodactylum tricornutum (Armbrust et al., Allen et al.) revealed the surprising presence of a complete, functional urea cycle in diatoms.
  • In diatoms, the urea cycle is integrated with the mitochondrial TCA cycle and chloroplast metabolism, serving not as an excretory mechanism, but as an essential anabolic hub for cellular nitrogen distribution, carbon recycling, and rapid metabolic recovery following periods of episodic nitrogen starvation.

question: Which of the following algae is responsible for the red color of RED SEA?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] The Red Sea Algal Bloom: Trichodesmium erythraeum:
  • Etiology of the Red Sea: The Red Sea derives its historic name from episodic, massive open-ocean blooms of the pelagic marine cyanobacterium Trichodesmium erythraeum (commonly called "sea sawdust").
  • Pigment Composition: Trichodesmium is a colonial, filamentous, diazotrophic cyanobacterium that forms large rafts on the ocean surface. It contains high amounts of the red accessory phycobiliprotein phycoerythrin.
  • When massive blooms senesce and collapse under calm conditions, the liberated phycoerythrin colors the seawater a vivid reddish-brown over thousands of square kilometers.

question: An oligotrophic lake has
options: High level of nutrients in water
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Limnological Classification of Lakes: Oligotrophic vs. Eutrophic:
  • Oligotrophic Lakes: Lakes characterized by very low concentrations of dissolved plant nutrients (nitrogen and phosphorus).
    • Because macronutrients are scarce, they support low primary productivity and low algal/plant biomass.
    • The water is crystal clear with very high Secchi depth transparency.
    • Due to low organic decomposition rates, dissolved oxygen levels remain high ($>80\text{--}100\%$ saturation) throughout the epilimnion and hypolimnion year-round.
  • Eutrophic lakes, by contrast, possess high nutrient levels, frequent algal blooms, high aquatic productivity, and deep-water anoxia.

question: After sodium chloride, which one of the following compounds has the maximum concentration in sea water?
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Salinity and Major Ionic Salts in Seawater:
  • At typical oceanic salinity ($35\text{ PSU}$ or $35\text{ g/kg}$ of seawater), dissolved mineral salts occur in the following proportions:
    1. Sodium Chloride ($\text{NaCl}$): Dominates seawater salts ($\,\sim 27.2\text{ g/kg}$, representing $\sim 78\%$ of all dissolved salts).
    2. Magnesium Chloride ($\text{MgCl}_2$): $\sim 3.8\text{ g/kg}$ (second most abundant compound).
    3. Magnesium Sulphate ($\text{MgSO}_4$): $\sim 1.7\text{ g/kg}$.
    4. Calcium Sulphate ($\text{CaSO}_4$): $\sim 1.3\text{ g/kg}$.
    5. Potassium Sulphate ($\text{K}_2\text{SO}_4$) / $\text{KCl}$: $\sim 0.9\text{ g/kg}$.
  • Note: In seawater chemical oceanography, $\text{NaCl}$ is followed by $\text{MgCl}_2$, with $\text{MgSO}_4$ third. The official exam answer key designated Option A (Magnesium sulphate). Both the chemical ranking and the official answer key designation are noted for clarity.

question: Which of the following is an example of an intellectual property right?
options: The deed to a plot of land
explanation:
[CONCEPT] Concept of Intellectual Property Rights (IPR):
  • Intellectual Property (IP): Refers to creations of the human mind/intellect—such as inventions, literary and artistic works, designs, symbols, names, and software.
  • Intellectual Property Rights: Legal rights that confer exclusive statutory protection to the creators or owners to control the commercial exploitation of their intangible creations:
    • The Copyright on a book: A classic, formal intellectual property right that legally protects the author's original expression and prevents unauthorized copying, reproduction, distribution, translation, or public performance.
    • A book that you own: A tangible personal property (physical chattel).
    • The deed to a plot of land: Real estate property (tangible real property).
    • An airline ticket: A personal commercial contract of carriage.
  • Therefore, the copyright on a book is an intellectual property right.
